entries.title: Roux, okra and filé
entries.summary: The three ways a Louisiana cook gives a gumbo its body: a roux of flour cooked in fat, okra cooked down until its sticky juice thickens the pot, and filé, ground sassafras leaves stirred in at the end.
entries.guest: Gumbo takes its body from a roux, from okra, from filé, which is ground sassafras leaves, or from a mix of them. I can ask the kitchen how tonight's is made.

paras: A gumbo is a soup that eats like a stew, and something has to give it that body. Louisiana cooks have three thickeners, and each brings flavour as well as texture. Roux is flour cooked in fat until it toasts. Okra is a green pod whose sticky juice thickens the pot as it simmers. Filé (FEE-lay) is the dried leaf of the sassafras tree, ground to a green powder and stirred in at the very end.

Nearly every modern gumbo starts on a roux, and many add okra or filé as well. The choice changes the bowl: roux gives toasty depth, okra a silky, faintly grassy body, filé an earthy, herbal note and a soft, velvety thickness.

Roux comes first. Cook oil and an equal weight of flour in a heavy pot, stirring without stopping, to the colour the dish wants, usually a deep brown for gumbo. The trinity, onion, celery and green pepper, goes straight into the hot roux: it cools the pot, stops the browning and softens in the fat. Stock follows a ladle at a time, whisked hard so no lumps form. Allow about 50 g (1.75 oz) of flour to 1 litre (about 1 quart) of stock: a generous measure for so thin a pot, because a dark roux thickens far less than a pale one, as the roux ladder explains.

Okra is sliced into rounds about 1 cm (3/8 inch) thick and smothered first: cooked down in a little oil over a medium heat, stirred often, for 20 to 30 minutes. At first it throws long, sticky strings, which cooks call the rope; this is its mucilage, a soluble fibre that thickens water. Cooking it down tames the rope, and a splash of tomato or vinegar helps. The okra then simmers in the gumbo for at least 30 minutes more, where what is left of its mucilage gives the pot body.

Filé goes in last, and never into a boiling pot. Take the gumbo off the heat and stir in 5 to 15 ml (1 to 3 tsp) for a pot for eight, or pass it at the table for a pinch a bowl. Boiled, filé turns a gumbo stringy and gluey, which is why many cooks add it bowl by bowl: the rest of the pot can then be reheated.

The old Creole households thickened with whatever the season gave. Okra is a summer crop, so summer brought okra gumbo, gombo févi in Creole French; sassafras leaves could be dried and pounded to keep, so the winter pot was a filé gumbo. Hence the old rule that okra and filé do not share a pot: they were the two halves of the year, and both thicken through a slippery mucilage, so together they can make a gumbo gluey. Many cooks break the rule today, Brennan's published recipe among them.

Thickening faults show at the spoon. A thin gumbo had too little roux for its colour, or okra that did not simmer long enough; a slimy one, okra that went in raw; a stringy, gluey one, filé that met the boil, which cannot be undone. A good gumbo coats a spoon lightly and still pours.

The Brennan's menu describes the Seafood Gumbo by its seafood, andouille and popcorn rice and names no thickener. The house's published recipe starts with a dark mahogany roux and carries okra, tomato and filé, but whether the dining room gumbo follows it is confirmed at lineup, so say published recipe, never menu. Okra is on the menu, but crisp: fried into chips on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits and worked into the tostada, where it thickens nothing.

Guests ask whether there is okra, whether it is thick and whether there is flour. Say what you know: a gumbo is usually built on a roux, and okra and filé are the other two thickeners. A guest who asks about flour or gluten goes straight to the kitchen, never to a guess. A guest who dislikes okra can be told that cooked down well it melts into the broth, and the kitchen can say whether it is in tonight's pot.

ratios.label: Dark roux for a gumbo
ratios.value: About 50 g (1.75 oz) of flour, in an equal weight of oil, to 1 litre (about 1 quart) of stock

ratios.label: Okra for a pot for eight
ratios.value: About 450 g (1 lb), sliced and smothered for 20 to 30 minutes first

ratios.label: Filé
ratios.value: 5 to 15 ml (1 to 3 tsp) for a pot for eight, off the heat, or a pinch a bowl at the table

faults.cause: Too little roux for how dark it was taken, or okra that did not simmer long enough.
faults.fix: Simmer it down, or whisk in a spoonful of roux made separately and simmer 15 minutes more.

faults.cause: The okra went in raw, or there was too much of it.
faults.fix: Smother sliced okra in fat until the strings cook away before it goes in; a splash of tomato or vinegar helps.

faults.cause: Filé was boiled, or added on top of plenty of okra.
faults.fix: It cannot be undone; next time stir filé in off the heat or pass it at the table.

faults.cause: Fat separating from the roux as the pot simmers.
faults.fix: Skim it with a ladle as it rises, and keep the pot at a gentle simmer rather than a hard boil.

brennans.how: The house's published gumbo recipe starts with a dark mahogany roux, the Creole tradition for gumbo. How dark the dining room roux goes, and whether the gumbo follows that recipe, are questions for the chef at lineup.
Okra on our menus is crisp, fried into chips on the Shrimp & Grits, so it adds crunch, never thickness. The menu does not list okra in the gumbo, so do not promise it there.

sources.title: A Short History of Gumbo, Stanley Dry, Southern Foodways Alliance

cards.front: What are the three classic thickeners of a gumbo?
cards.back: Roux, flour cooked in fat; okra, cooked down until its juice thickens the pot; and filé, ground dried sassafras leaves.

cards.front: When does the roux go into a gumbo, and what stops it browning?
cards.back: It is made first, in the pot; the trinity goes straight into the hot roux, which cools it and halts the browning.

cards.front: How much roux does a pot of gumbo take, and how should the finished pot look?
cards.back: About 50 g (1.75 oz) of flour, in an equal weight of oil, to 1 litre (about 1 quart) of stock, a generous measure because dark roux thickens less. The gumbo should coat a spoon lightly and still pour.

cards.front: What is okra's rope, and how do cooks tame it?
cards.back: The sticky strings of its mucilage, a soluble fibre. Smothering sliced okra in fat for 20 to 30 minutes cooks the rope down before it goes in.

cards.front: What is filé, and what does it bring to a gumbo?
cards.back: The dried leaves of the sassafras tree, ground to a green powder; it thickens gently and adds an earthy, herbal note.

cards.front: Why is filé stirred in off the heat or passed at the table?
cards.back: Boiled, it turns the gumbo stringy and gluey; added bowl by bowl, it also leaves the rest of the pot free to be reheated.

cards.front: What is the old rule about okra and filé?
cards.back: Not both in one pot: they were the summer and winter thickeners, and together their slippery mucilage can make a gumbo gluey.

cards.front: Why was okra gumbo a summer dish and filé gumbo a winter one?
cards.back: Okra is a summer crop, while sassafras leaves could be dried and pounded to keep through the cold months.

cards.front: A gumbo turned stringy and gluey once the filé went in. What happened?
cards.back: The filé met the boil. It cannot be undone; next time add it off the heat or pass it at the table.

cards.front: What may a server say about how the Brennan's gumbo is thickened?
cards.back: The menu names no thickener. The published recipe starts on a dark roux and carries okra, tomato and filé; confirm at lineup before saying so.

cards.front: A guest asks whether the gumbo has flour in it. What do you do?
cards.back: Say a gumbo is usually built on a roux, then take the question to the kitchen; flour and gluten questions are never answered by guesswork.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the three classic gumbo thickeners?
distractors: A slurry of cornflour and water
Reduced double cream
Puréed white beans
questions.why: Filé, ground dried sassafras leaves, stands with roux and okra as the three traditional ways to give a gumbo body.

questions.q: A guest asks whether the gumbo is made with flour. What do you do?
questions.answer: Say it is usually roux-built, then ask the kitchen
distractors: Say no, because okra and filé thicken it instead
Judge from how thick the broth looks, then answer
Tell them a dark roux has no flour left in it
questions.why: Nearly every gumbo starts on a roux of flour and fat, but only the kitchen can answer for tonight's pot, so flour and gluten questions go there.

questions.q: How should a gumbo thickened to the right body behave on a spoon?
questions.answer: It coats the spoon lightly and still pours
distractors: It stands up in a stiff mound
It runs off clear, like a broth
It hangs from the spoon in ropy strings
questions.why: A gumbo is a soup that eats like a stew. Stiff means too much thickening, clear and runny too little, and ropy strings mean okra not cooked down or filé that boiled.

questions.q: Why do cooks smother sliced okra in fat before it goes into the gumbo?
questions.answer: To cook down its sticky rope
distractors: To brown it as dark as the roux
To soften its tough, woody seeds
To boil off its bitter green juice
questions.why: Smothering cooks away the long strings of mucilage, so the okra softens into the broth and thickens it without slime.

questions.q: Why is filé added off the heat or at the table rather than boiled in the pot?
questions.answer: Boiling turns it stringy and gluey
distractors: It would sink and scorch on the bottom
It only dissolves in cold liquid
Heat drives off all its thickening
questions.why: Filé thickens gently once the pot is off the boil; boiled, its mucilage turns ropy and the gumbo goes gluey.

questions.q: What is the old rule about using okra and filé in the same gumbo?
questions.answer: Use one or the other, not both
distractors: Always use both, in equal parts
Filé first, then okra on top
Neither may go with seafood
questions.why: They were the summer and winter thickeners, and together their slippery mucilage can make a gumbo gluey.

questions.q: In the old Creole households, when was filé gumbo usually made?
questions.answer: In winter, when okra was out of season
distractors: In summer, at the height of okra season
Only on Good Friday
Only for wedding feasts
questions.why: Okra is a summer crop; sassafras leaves could be dried and pounded to keep, so filé thickened the winter pot.

questions.q: What does the Brennan's menu say about how its Seafood Gumbo is thickened?
distractors: That it is thickened with okra alone
That filé is passed at the table
That it is built on a white roux
questions.why: The menu names no thickener; the published recipe carries roux, okra and filé, and the dining room build is confirmed at lineup.

entries.title: Seafood gumbo
entries.summary: A New Orleans classic: Gulf shrimp, blue crab and oysters in a dark broth built on roux, the trinity and a stock of shells, often with tomato and smoked sausage, the seafood added last and served over rice.
entries.guest: Our Seafood Gumbo is shrimp, crab and oysters with smoky andouille over Louisiana popcorn rice: savoury, briny and gently smoky.

paras: Seafood gumbo is a New Orleans classic: a dark, brothy stew of Gulf shrimp, blue crab and oysters, built on a roux and the trinity and served over rice. It is Creole cooking at its most typical, a French roux, West African okra and the catch of the coast in one pot.

Its whole skill is timing. The base of roux, vegetables, stock and seasoning wants an hour or more to come together; the seafood wants minutes. A good seafood gumbo is built so the two meet at the last moment.

Make the stock first: shrimp shells and heads and cleaned blue crab bodies, simmered with onion trimmings, celery and bay for 20 to 30 minutes, then strained. In a heavy pot, cook oil and flour to a dark roux, stir in the trinity, onion, celery and green pepper, and cook until soft before the garlic goes in for a minute. Sliced andouille or smoked sausage, browned first in many kitchens, brings smoke and depth.

Whisk in the hot stock a ladle at a time, about 3 litres (about 3 quarts) for a pot for eight, then add tomato if the cook uses it, with bay, thyme, cayenne and black pepper. In the Creole tradition, okra, smothered first, goes in now. Simmer gently for about an hour, skimming the oil that rises, until the broth coats a spoon lightly and the flavours have married.

The seafood goes in last, in order of how long it needs. Shrimp take 2 to 3 minutes, until they turn pink and curl. Picked crab claws and lump crabmeat, the large pieces of body meat, are sold cooked, so they are only warmed through. Oysters and their liquor, the briny juice from the shell, go in at the very end and are done as soon as their edges curl, a minute or so. Off the heat, check the salt; filé, for the cooks who use it, is stirred in now or passed at the table.

The faults come from heat and time. Rubbery shrimp and shrunken, leathery oysters mean the seafood cooked too long, usually because the whole pot was held hot after it went in. That is why some kitchens hold the base on its own and add the seafood to each batch, or even each order, so it meets the heat for minutes. Lump crab falls into threads if stirred hard; fold it in. A bitter, burnt taste means the roux scorched, and nothing hides it. Cooling and keeping a pot follow the kitchen's own rules.

Reheating follows the same rule. Bring a held base back to a gentle simmer before the seafood goes in. A pot reheated with its seafood already in is warmed slowly, stirred gently so the crab stays whole, and served as soon as it is hot, never brought to the boil.

The Brennan's Seafood Gumbo has its own entry; here it shows the method at work. The menu names shrimp, crab and oysters with andouille over Louisiana popcorn rice, and the house's published recipe adds the seafood at the very end so it stays tender. Whether the dining room follows that recipe is a lineup question.

Seafood gumbo is served in a bowl over a mound of rice, never cooked with the rice, and finished with sliced green onion (spring onion) and chopped parsley. Tell the guest what is in it in plain words: shrimp, crab, oysters and smoked sausage in a rich, savoury broth. Asked whether the Brennan's gumbo is spicy, the house answer is mild to moderate. Questions about shellfish, pork or how the gumbo is thickened go to the kitchen.

ratios.label: Stock for a pot for eight
ratios.value: About 3 litres (about 3 quarts) of shrimp and crab stock

ratios.label: Dark roux for that pot
ratios.value: About 150 g (5 oz) of flour in an equal weight of oil

ratios.label: Seafood timing
ratios.value: Shrimp 2 to 3 minutes; cooked crab only warmed; oysters until the edges curl, about a minute

faults.cause: Cooked too long, often held hot in the pot after they went in.
faults.fix: Add shrimp for the last 2 to 3 minutes only, or to each batch or order.

faults.cause: Boiled, or held hot after they went in.
faults.fix: Add them with their liquor at the very end and serve as soon as the edges curl.

faults.cause: Lump crabmeat stirred hard or simmered.
faults.fix: Fold it in gently at the end and warm it only.
Nothing hides it; start a new roux.

faults.cause: Too short a simmer, or the fat was never skimmed.
faults.fix: Simmer gently for the full hour, skimming as the oil rises.

components: Louisiana blue crab and lump crabmeat
brennans.how: Shrimp, crab and oysters are the gumbo's seafood, and the house's published recipe adds them at the very end so they stay tender. Confirm at lineup that the dining room gumbo follows it before saying so to a guest.
Andouille, a coarse, smoked pork sausage, gives the gumbo its smoky backbone under the seafood. Tell a guest who avoids pork that it is in the gumbo before they order.

components: Louisiana blue crab and lump crabmeat

cards.front: What is a Creole seafood gumbo?
cards.back: A dark, brothy stew of shrimp, crab and oysters built on a roux and the trinity, simmered in a stock of shells and served over rice.

cards.front: What stock does a seafood gumbo use, and what is it made from?
cards.back: A quick stock of shrimp shells and heads and cleaned blue crab bodies, simmered with aromatics for 20 to 30 minutes and strained.

cards.front: Which seasonings does a Creole seafood gumbo often carry?
cards.back: Garlic, bay, thyme, cayenne and black pepper, and often tomato, which marks it as a Creole pot rather than a Cajun one.

cards.front: Why do many seafood gumbos carry andouille or smoked sausage?
cards.back: For smoke and depth under the sweet seafood; it is browned and simmered in the base, so its flavour runs through the broth.

cards.front: In what order does the seafood go into the pot?
cards.back: At the end, by cooking time: shrimp for 2 to 3 minutes, then the cooked crab to warm, then the oysters and their liquor until the edges curl.

cards.front: How do you know the oysters in a gumbo are done?
cards.back: Their edges curl, usually within a minute; a moment longer and they shrink and toughen.

cards.front: Why is lump crabmeat only warmed in a gumbo, never simmered?
cards.back: It is already cooked, and simmering or hard stirring breaks it into threads and dulls its sweetness.

cards.front: Where do okra and filé sit in a seafood gumbo?
cards.back: Okra, smothered first, simmers in the base in the Creole tradition; filé, where used, goes in off the heat or is passed at the table.

cards.front: How do kitchens hold seafood gumbo without overcooking the seafood?
cards.back: Some hold the base on its own and add the seafood to each batch or order, so it meets the heat for only minutes; a pot reheated with its seafood in is warmed gently, never boiled.

cards.front: How is a bowl of seafood gumbo served?
cards.back: Over a mound of rice cooked separately, never in the pot, topped with sliced green onion and chopped parsley.

cards.front: What does the Brennan's published gumbo recipe do with the seafood, and how do you mention it?
cards.back: It adds the shrimp, crab and oysters at the very end so they stay tender. Say published recipe, never menu, and only once lineup confirms the dining room gumbo follows it.

cards.front: A guest who avoids pork asks about the Brennan's Seafood Gumbo. What do you say?
cards.back: Before they order, tell them andouille, a smoked pork sausage, is in the gumbo, and take any further question to the kitchen.

questions.q: What is the stock of a seafood gumbo usually made from?
distractors: Roasted veal bones
Smoked ham hocks alone
Dried mushrooms and kombu seaweed
questions.why: The shells and crab bodies give a quick, sweet stock of the sea that ties the broth to the seafood that goes in at the end.

questions.q: Which of the seafood goes into a seafood gumbo last?
distractors: The peeled shrimp, still raw
The picked crab claws
The lump crabmeat, folded in
questions.why: Oysters need only a minute, until their edges curl, so they go in at the very end with the briny juice from the shell, after the shrimp have cooked and the crab has warmed through.

questions.q: How does a cook know the oysters in a gumbo are done?
distractors: They sink to the bottom
They turn bright orange
They split open
questions.why: Curling edges show the oyster has just set; a moment longer and it shrinks and turns leathery.

questions.q: Why is lump crabmeat only warmed through in a gumbo?
questions.answer: It is already cooked and shreds easily
distractors: Long heat turns its sweet meat bitter
Boiled, it would thicken the broth
It is raw and cooks in the hot bowl
questions.why: Picked lump crab is sold cooked; simmering or stirring hard shreds it and dulls its sweetness.

questions.q: How do some kitchens keep the seafood in a gumbo from overcooking through service?
questions.answer: Hold the base; add seafood to each batch
distractors: Simmer the full pot hard all service
Poach the seafood the night before
Add extra roux to shield the seafood
questions.why: The base improves with holding and the seafood does not, so the seafood is added close to service and meets the heat for minutes.

questions.q: In the Creole tradition, when does smothered okra go into a seafood gumbo?
questions.answer: With the stock, for the long simmer
distractors: With the oysters, at the very end
Raw, straight into the hot roux
At the table, as a pinch a bowl
questions.why: Smothered okra simmers in the base so its body thickens the pot; filé, not okra, is the thickener passed at the table.

questions.q: What does andouille bring to a seafood gumbo?
questions.answer: Smoke and depth under the seafood
distractors: Most of the gumbo's thickening
A sharp, pickled vinegar note
Sweetness from a cane syrup glaze
questions.why: Andouille is a coarse, smoked pork sausage; browned and simmered in the base, it gives the broth a smoky backbone.

questions.q: What should a guest who avoids pork hear about the Brennan's Seafood Gumbo before ordering?
questions.answer: Andouille, a pork sausage, is in it
distractors: It is all seafood, with no meat at all
The pork is only in the stock
The andouille is served on the side
questions.why: Andouille, a smoked pork sausage, is part of the Seafood Gumbo, so a guest who avoids pork hears it before ordering; anything further goes to the kitchen.

entries.title: Gumbo z'herbes
entries.summary: Green gumbo: an odd number of greens, collards, mustard, turnip tops, spinach and cabbage among them, cooked down and chopped or puréed. Once a meatless Lenten dish, it is now the rich Holy Thursday gumbo of New Orleans.
entries.guest: Gumbo z'herbes is green gumbo, many kinds of greens cooked down with smoked meats and served over rice, the traditional New Orleans dish for Holy Thursday.

paras: Gumbo z'herbes is green gumbo: a pot of many greens, collards, mustard greens, turnip tops, spinach, cabbage and more, simmered soft, then chopped fine or puréed and cooked on in their own liquor until the broth turns deep green. Where most gumbos are about seafood or poultry, this one is about the garden.
The name is New Orleans French. Gumbo aux herbes, gumbo with greens, runs together in speech so that the x of aux is sounded as a z on the front of herbes: z'herbes.

Wash the greens in several changes of cold water, lifting them out so the grit stays behind, and strip the tough stems. Simmer them in salted water or light stock, the sturdy collards first and the tender spinach last, until all are soft, 30 to 45 minutes. Lift them out, keep every drop of the cooking liquor, and chop the greens fine or purée them.

Brown the meats in the pot: smoked sausage, ham and fresh hot sausage are common, and some cooks add brisket or chicken. If the recipe uses a roux, make it in that fat, add onion and garlic, then return the greens with enough liquor for a thick, soupy stew. Season with thyme, bay and cayenne, and simmer for about an hour, stirring often, because puréed greens settle and catch on the bottom. Serve over rice.

Versions part on two questions. Roux or none: older pots often took their body from the puréed greens alone, while many modern cooks start on a roux. Meat or none: the Lenten pot was meatless, while the Holy Thursday pot carries smoked sausage, ham and more. Okra is rare; filé sometimes finishes it. Its cousins are the leafy green stews of West Africa and the Caribbean, such as callaloo, cooked with greens and often salted meat, crab or smoked fish, which makes the pot as much African as French, whatever its name.

In the old Catholic households of New Orleans, gumbo z'herbes was a Lenten dish, made without meat for Good Friday, when Catholics fasted and went without meat. In time it moved to Holy Thursday, the day before, and filled up with meat, a feast before the fast rather than the fast itself.

The pot that made the custom famous was Leah Chase's at Dooky Chase's Restaurant, made once a year for Holy Thursday. She insisted on an uneven number of greens, nine in her recipe, and the custom is told this way: each green stands for a new friend in the year ahead, and an odd number brings luck.

Grit in the bowl means the greens were not washed well enough. A harsh, bitter pot has too much mustard or turnip for its milder greens; balance it with cabbage or spinach and season well, since salt tames bitterness. A scorched taste means the thick purée sat on the heat unstirred.

Our gumbo is the seafood one, so gumbo z'herbes comes to the table as a question, most often in Lent. Describe it plainly: many greens cooked down, rich with smoked meats in its Holy Thursday form, served over rice. A guest who asks whether a gumbo z'herbes is vegetarian should hear that most modern versions carry meat, and that only the kitchen that made a pot can answer for it.

ratios.label: Greens for a pot for ten
ratios.value: About 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) of mixed raw greens

ratios.label: Number of greens
ratios.value: An odd number, often seven or nine; nine in Leah Chase's recipe, though published lists of her nine vary

ratios.label: Cooking times
ratios.value: Greens 30 to 45 minutes; the finished gumbo about an hour more

faults.cause: The leaves were not washed well enough.
faults.fix: Wash in several changes of cold water, lifting the greens out so the grit stays behind.

faults.cause: Too high a share of mustard or turnip greens.
faults.fix: Balance with milder greens such as cabbage and spinach, and season well with salt.

faults.cause: Puréed greens are thick and settle on the heat.
faults.fix: Use a heavy pot, keep the heat low and stir often.

faults.cause: Too much cooking liquor added back at once.
faults.fix: Add the liquor a ladle at a time, or simmer the pot down.

cards.front: What is gumbo z'herbes?
cards.back: Green gumbo: many kinds of greens simmered soft, chopped or puréed and cooked on in their liquor, usually with smoked meats, served over rice.

cards.front: Name five greens commonly found in gumbo z'herbes.
cards.back: Collards, mustard greens, turnip tops, spinach and cabbage; cooks add others such as watercress, beet tops and parsley.

cards.front: Where does the name z'herbes come from?
cards.back: From the French aux herbes, with greens: said quickly, the x of aux is sounded as a z on the front of herbes, giving z'herbes.

cards.front: Why was gumbo z'herbes once made without meat?
cards.back: It was a Lenten dish of the Catholic households, cooked to be eaten on Good Friday, when Catholics went without meat.

cards.front: On which day is gumbo z'herbes now traditionally eaten in New Orleans?
cards.back: Holy Thursday, the day before Good Friday, when it is usually made rich with smoked meats and sausage.

cards.front: Why does a gumbo z'herbes use an odd number of greens?
cards.back: For luck: the custom says each green stands for a new friend in the coming year, and an odd number brings good fortune.

cards.front: Whose Holy Thursday gumbo z'herbes made the custom famous?
cards.back: Leah Chase's, at Dooky Chase's Restaurant in New Orleans, made once a year with an uneven number of greens, nine in her recipe.

cards.front: What are the cousins of gumbo z'herbes outside Louisiana?
cards.back: The leafy green stews of West Africa and the Caribbean, such as callaloo, cooked with greens and often salted meat, crab or smoked fish.

cards.front: Does a gumbo z'herbes use a roux?
cards.back: Some do and some do not: older pots often took their body from the puréed greens alone, while many modern cooks start on a roux.

cards.front: How are the greens cooked for gumbo z'herbes?
cards.back: Simmered soft, sturdy greens first, for 30 to 45 minutes, then lifted out, chopped or puréed and returned to their own cooking liquor.

cards.front: Why must a gumbo z'herbes be stirred often as it simmers?
cards.back: Puréed greens are thick and settle, so they catch and scorch on the bottom of the pot unless the heat is low and the spoon keeps moving.

questions.q: What does z'herbes mean in the name gumbo z'herbes?
distractors: Without meat
For Good Friday
With roux
questions.why: Gumbo aux herbes means gumbo with greens; said quickly, the x of aux sounds as a z on herbes. Meatless was its Lenten form, not its name.

questions.q: Why was gumbo z'herbes once a meatless dish?
questions.answer: It was made for Good Friday in Lent
distractors: Meat was too costly in summer
Greens and meat were thought to clash
It was a dish for invalids
questions.why: Catholic households went without meat on Good Friday, so the green gumbo was their Lenten pot before it moved to Holy Thursday.

questions.q: On which day is gumbo z'herbes now traditionally served in New Orleans?
distractors: Mardi Gras day
Easter Monday
Christmas Eve
questions.why: It moved from the Good Friday fast to the day before, where it became a feast rich with smoked meats.

questions.q: Why do many cooks use an odd number of greens in gumbo z'herbes?
questions.answer: For luck, each green a new friend
distractors: So the pot cooks more evenly
Because greens are sold in threes
To keep the gumbo from turning bitter
questions.why: The custom says each green brings a new friend in the year ahead, and an odd number brings luck; Leah Chase used nine.

questions.q: Which New Orleans chef made a Holy Thursday gumbo z'herbes famous at her family's restaurant?
distractors: Ella Brennan
Lena Richard
Susan Spicer
questions.why: Leah Chase cooked it once a year for Holy Thursday at Dooky Chase's Restaurant, always with an uneven number of greens.

questions.q: Which dish is a Caribbean cousin of gumbo z'herbes?
distractors: Paella
Ratatouille
Bouillabaisse
questions.why: Callaloo is a stew of leafy greens, often with salted meat or crab, from the same West African family of green pots.

questions.q: How do versions of gumbo z'herbes differ over roux?
questions.answer: Many use one; older pots often did not
distractors: The roux must go darker than any gumbo's
The roux is stirred in raw at the end
Only the Good Friday pot takes a roux
questions.why: The puréed greens give body of their own, so older recipes often skipped the roux, while many modern cooks start on one.

questions.q: Why must a pot of gumbo z'herbes be stirred often as it simmers?
distractors: It keeps the greens bright green
It cools the pot so it never boils
It helps the filé dissolve
questions.why: The thick purée sinks and catches on the bottom of the pot, so low heat and a moving spoon keep it from burning.

entries.title: Étouffée
entries.summary: Smothered: crawfish tails or shrimp in a thick, buttery sauce of blond to peanut butter roux, the trinity and a little shell stock, spooned over rice. A sauce rather than a soup, and in its crawfish form a Cajun classic.
entries.guest: Étouffée means smothered: crawfish or shrimp in a thick, buttery sauce with onion, celery and pepper, spooned over rice, with a gentle heat.

paras: Étouffée means smothered. Crawfish tails or shrimp are cooked in a thick, glossy sauce of butter, the trinity and a little stock, just enough to coat them, and the dish is spooned over rice. It is a sauce, not a soup: where a gumbo is ladled, an étouffée sits on the rice and holds its shape for a moment before it settles.
In its crawfish form it is a Cajun classic, built on the sweet tail meat and the golden fat of crawfish in their spring season.

Simmer the crawfish or shrimp shells in water with onion trimmings and bay for 20 to 30 minutes for a quick stock, and strain it. Crawfish tails are usually bought cooked and peeled, packed with their fat, so a crawfish étouffée often uses a light shrimp or seafood stock instead. Melt butter in a wide, heavy pan, about 115 g (4 oz) for each 450 g (1 lb) of tails, stir in 30 g (1 oz) of flour and cook it to blond or peanut butter brown, 10 to 20 minutes over a medium heat. Add the trinity, onion, celery and green pepper, soften it, then add the garlic.

Whisk in the stock a little at a time, only about 350 ml (about 1.5 cups) for each 450 g (1 lb) of tails, so the sauce coats a spoon heavily. Season with cayenne, black pepper and salt and simmer for 15 to 20 minutes. Add the tails with their fat, or the shrimp, for 3 to 5 minutes, only until hot through or pink. Finish with sliced green onion and chopped parsley, and serve over white rice.

The yellow-orange crawfish fat is not true fat but the hepatopancreas, a fat-rich organ that digests the crawfish's food. It carries much of the flavour and colours the sauce gold, so a Cajun cook would never rinse it away.

Étouffée has two main lines. The Cajun crawfish étouffée of the Breaux Bridge country is blond to pale brown, buttery and usually made without tomato, its colour from the fat; Creole cooks in the city often add tomato, which reddens it and gives an acid edge. Some cooks make no roux at all and let butter, crawfish fat and reduced stock thicken it, a richer, looser sauce.

Know it against its neighbours. A gumbo is a soup, with a darker roux and far more liquid; an étouffée is a thick sauce on a lighter roux. A Cajun stew or fricassée goes the other way, a darker roux and a gravy loose enough to ladle, while an étouffée is smothered thick.

Breaux Bridge, in St. Martin Parish, holds the Cajun claim. The history 64 Parishes tells credits the Hébert sisters, Yolie and Marie, whose parents ran the town's Hébert Hotel in the 1920s, with an early version they called a crawfish courtbouillon, and Aline Guidry Champagne with the version that took the name. In the late 1940s she left out the tomato, garlic and celery, told guests in her kitchen she was smothering the crawfish, and the dish went on the Rendezvous Club menu in 1950. The legislature named Breaux Bridge the Crawfish Capital of the World in 1959.

Describe it plainly: crawfish tails, or shrimp, smothered in a thick butter sauce with onion, celery and pepper, over rice, with a gentle heat. Our menu carries no étouffée; the house's crawfish dish is the Crawfish Meat Pies at the Roost, and how their filling is made is not printed, so ask the kitchen before describing it. Questions about shellfish, butter or flour in any dish go to the kitchen.

ratios.label: Butter and flour for 450 g (1 lb) of tails
ratios.value: About 115 g (4 oz) of butter and 30 g (1 oz) of flour

ratios.label: Stock
ratios.value: About 350 ml (about 1.5 cups) for each 450 g (1 lb) of tails

ratios.label: Roux colour
ratios.value: Blond to peanut butter, 10 to 20 minutes over a medium heat

ratios.label: Tails in the sauce
ratios.value: 3 to 5 minutes, only until hot through

faults.cause: Too much stock for the roux.
faults.fix: Reduce it before the tails go in; it should coat a spoon heavily.

faults.fault: Tough, shrunken tails or rubbery shrimp
faults.cause: Cooked too long in the sauce.
faults.fix: Add them last and heat through for 3 to 5 minutes only.

faults.cause: Boiled hard, or too little liquid for the butter.
faults.fix: Whisk in a spoonful of hot stock and keep the pan at a gentle simmer.

faults.cause: The milk solids in butter scorch sooner than oil does.
faults.fix: Cook over a medium heat and stir without stopping; start again if it flecks black.

faults.cause: The crawfish fat was rinsed away, or the pot was under-seasoned.
faults.fix: Keep the fat with the tails and season with cayenne and salt at the end.

cards.front: What does étouffée mean, and what is the dish?
cards.back: Smothered: crawfish or shrimp cooked in a thick sauce of butter, roux, the trinity and a little stock, served over rice.

cards.front: How dark is the roux for an étouffée?
cards.back: Blond to peanut butter, lighter than a gumbo's, usually made in butter and cooked 10 to 20 minutes over a medium heat.

cards.front: What is crawfish fat, and why does a Cajun cook keep it?
cards.back: The yellow-orange hepatopancreas, the crawfish's digestive organ; it carries much of the flavour and colours the sauce gold.

cards.front: How much stock goes into an étouffée, and what is it made from?
cards.back: Little: about 350 ml (about 1.5 cups) for each 450 g (1 lb) of tails, from simmered crawfish or shrimp shells, so the sauce stays thick.

cards.front: When do the tails go into an étouffée, and for how long?
cards.back: Last, for 3 to 5 minutes, only until hot through; any longer and they shrink and toughen.

cards.front: Which town holds the Cajun claim to crawfish étouffée?
cards.back: Breaux Bridge, in St. Martin Parish, which the Louisiana legislature named the Crawfish Capital of the World in 1959.

cards.front: Who is credited with giving crawfish étouffée its name in Breaux Bridge, and when?
cards.back: Aline Guidry Champagne, in the late 1940s, who told guests she was smothering the crawfish; it went on the Rendezvous Club menu in 1950.

cards.front: How does a Creole étouffée often differ from a Cajun one?
cards.back: Creole cooks often add tomato, for a redder, sharper sauce; the Cajun crawfish version is buttery and usually made without tomato, gold from the fat.

cards.front: How can an étouffée be thickened without a roux?
cards.back: With butter, crawfish fat and reduced stock alone, which gives a richer, looser sauce than the roux-based style.

cards.front: How does an étouffée differ from a gumbo?
cards.back: It is a thick sauce on a lighter roux, spooned over rice; a gumbo is a soup with a darker roux and far more liquid.

cards.front: How does an étouffée differ from a Cajun stew or fricassée?
cards.back: A stew or fricassée takes a darker roux and more gravy, loose enough to ladle; an étouffée is lighter and smothered thick.

cards.front: How is an étouffée seasoned and finished?
cards.back: Seasoned with cayenne, black pepper and salt, finished with sliced green onion and chopped parsley, and served over white rice.

questions.q: What does the French word étouffée mean in a Louisiana kitchen?
distractors: Fried crisp
Boiled whole
Stuffed
questions.why: The crawfish or shrimp are smothered in a thick sauce that just coats them, which is the whole idea of the dish.

questions.q: Which roux colour suits a classic étouffée?
distractors: White, as pale as the flour
Dark chocolate, like old brick
Black, a shade past brick
questions.why: A lighter roux keeps the sauce buttery and lets the crawfish lead; the dark rungs belong to gumbo and stews.

questions.q: What is the yellow crawfish fat prized in a Cajun étouffée?
distractors: Fat rendered from the tail muscle meat
Roe, the eggs carried under the tail
Butter the frozen tails are packed in
questions.why: The hepatopancreas carries much of the crawfish's flavour and colours the sauce gold, so Cajun cooks keep every bit.

questions.q: How long do cooked crawfish tails need once they go into the sauce?
distractors: About an hour, to soften them
30 minutes at a full boil
Overnight in the fridge
questions.why: The tails are already cooked; more heat only shrinks and toughens them, so they go in last and come out hot.

questions.q: Which town did the Louisiana legislature name the Crawfish Capital of the World in 1959?
distractors: Gonzales
LaPlace
St. Martinville
questions.why: Breaux Bridge, in St. Martin Parish, is where the crawfish étouffée of the Hébert and Champagne kitchens took hold.

questions.q: What do Creole cooks often add to an étouffée that the Cajun crawfish version leaves out?
distractors: Butter
Cayenne
Green onion
questions.why: Tomato reddens a Creole étouffée and gives it an acid edge; the Cajun crawfish version takes its gold colour from the fat.

questions.q: How does an étouffée differ from a gumbo?
distractors: Thinner, with a darker roux
Thicker, with a darker roux
Thinner, with a lighter roux
questions.why: An étouffée is a thick sauce on a blond to peanut butter roux; a gumbo is a soup on a darker roux.

questions.q: Compared with an étouffée, what does a Cajun stew or fricassée usually have?
questions.answer: A darker roux and more gravy
distractors: A lighter roux and less gravy
A darker roux and less gravy
A lighter roux and more gravy
questions.why: Stews and fricassées take a darker roux and a looser gravy; an étouffée is lighter in colour and smothered thick.

questions.q: How is a roux-less étouffée thickened?
questions.answer: By butter, crawfish fat and reduced stock
distractors: By okra cooked down until it ropes
By filé stirred in at a full boil
By a cornflour slurry stirred in at the end
questions.why: Without flour, the butter, the crawfish fat and a well-reduced stock give the sauce its body, richer and looser than a roux sauce.
